summary: FindY is a geospatial intelligence web platform that lets researchers pick any location on the Moon or Mars and instantly discover its closest geological and environmental analogs on Earth. Testing rovers, life-support systems and planetary hardware in space is extremely expensive: a Moon base would cost about $10,800/kg to launch, based on Falcon Heavy’s $1,520/kg and a gear ratio of 7.2. Scientists also lack automated, multi-parameter tools for finding high-fidelity Earth analog sites. FindY addresses the challenge by comparing measured terrain from NASA’s MOLA and LOLA datasets (slope, local relief, roughness, elevation) with Earth data, then returning several ranked analog sites with a similarity score from 0 to 100 and a side-by-side comparison. For example, Mars’ Gale crater region matches Chile’s Atacama at 96.9. This helps teams test hardware on Earth more cheaply, flexibly and safely before committing to costly space missions.
details:
What it does and how it works. 

The user chooses Mars or the Moon, then selects a cell on an interactive surface map. The user can also apply manual scientific filters (slope P90, mean elevation, local relief, roughness RMS) or use an AI query. Dynamic filtering removes unsuitable regions and highlights the best matching cells. FindY then compares the chosen terrain against prepared Earth grid patches (about 500 per query) and returns the best patch per region, ranked by similarity score. Each result shows the Earth site on a satellite map with a measurement table (Moon/Mars vs. Earth vs. difference). Examples: a Moon site at 85.3° S matched McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica (83.4/100), and a Mars site matched Atacama, Chile (96.9/100). The results also include other candidates such as the Danakil Depression, Kangerlussuaq, Tongariro, and Oymyakon basin.

Benefits. 

FindY saves launch and testing costs by moving field tests to Earth. It replaces slow manual searching with an automated, multi-parameter, reproducible method. It also gives several ranked options instead of a single guess, and it is transparent about limitations: scores are screening values, not validation, and field verification is still required.

Intended impact. 

The target users are planetary scientists, aerospace engineers, rover mission teams, and Kazakh researchers. We want FindY to speed up mission preparation and make analog research accessible to teams without large budgets, including researchers in Kazakhstan, where the country’s varied terrain could host candidate analog sites.

Tools, languages, hardware and software. 

AI tools: CodeX and Claude for debugging and ML. Data sources: NASA MOLA (Mars) and LOLA (Moon) topography, USGS geologic maps of Mars and the Moon, Copernicus DEM GLO-30/90, NASA SRTM, ESA WorldCover 10m, NASA POWER and MERRA-2 climate data, the GLiM global lithological map, and USGS Cinder Lake analog site data.

Creativity.

 FindY reverses the usual workflow: instead of describing an Earth site and hoping it resembles space, the researcher starts from a specific lunar or Martian location and gets its “Earthly twin”. It combines authentic planetary cartography, quantitative terrain matching, an AI query option, and an interactive side-by-side comparison in one tool.

Factors we considered.

Cost: launch cost and mission gear ratios, which make in-space testing prohibitive.

Data comparability: matching terrain at comparable ground scales (sampling footprints within 15% per axis), despite different native DEM resolutions.

Scientific honesty: similarity scores are screening tools, and they don’t establish climate, geology, safety or accessibility on their own.

Coverage: geographically incomplete sampling can miss closer matches.

Users: scientists, engineers and rover teams need clear, ranked, verifiable results.
